title: Bloodwoods
scientificName: Corymbia clarksoniana, C. erythrophloia, C. hylandii, C. stockeri, C. terminalis and others

identification.basis: The dictionary gives three bloodwood words without saying which trees they are. Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas of Living Australia records seven rough-barked bloodwoods, led by Clarkson's bloodwood, which the Queensland Herbarium names as a main tree of the hill woodland here; which word goes with which tree is not recorded.

summary: The bloodwoods are the rough-barked gums of the [woodland](entry:woodland), named for the dark red kino that bleeds from a cut, and the dictionary has three words for them: **[babajaka](word:babajaka)**, **[kawarr](word:kawarr)** and **[kuji-kuji](word:kuji-kuji)**, each 'a species of bloodwood tree' [ref:hershberger1982]. At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) they are the second family of the hills after the ironbarks: Clarkson's bloodwood is one of the three trees the Queensland Herbarium names for the woodland on these slopes, and the Atlas of Living Australia records Hyland's, red, blotchy and inland bloodwoods as well within 30 km of the homestead [ref:re-woodland] [ref:ala-karma-plants]. They are known by their bark, 'tessellated', broken into small squares like a crocodile's back, and by their big urn- or barrel-shaped fruit [ref:euclid-clarksoniana] [ref:wiki-erythrophloia]. The old uses on record are the bark, which Roth saw made into pleated troughs at Cooktown, the boughs thrown down as a windbreak, the seed pods that Bloomfield people worked into their hair with beeswax and clay, the charcoal, the red gum as a medicine in the western and Palmer districts, and two foods Edward Palmer recorded on the Mitchell in 1883: the sweet manna that falls from the leaves after the rains, and the galls, 'Kurcha', with a grub or a bag of jelly inside [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910-huts] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1903] [ref:palmer1883]. The red-tailed black cockatoos that crack the fruit and the sugarbag bees in the hollows depend on the same trees [ref:wiki-rtbc].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[babajaka](word:babajaka)**, **[kawarr](word:kawarr)** and **[kuji-kuji](word:kuji-kuji)** are each glossed 'species of bloodwood tree' and nothing more, so the three words are three bloodwoods that the dictionary's speakers told apart and the dictionary does not [ref:hershberger1982]. Beside them the dictionary has **[kayjurr](word:kayjurr)** 'white gum', **[jabarr](word:jabarr)** 'baldy gum', **[dari](word:dari)** 'boxwood tree, grows mainly in high places', the stringybarks **[marbaji](word:marbaji)** and **[warka](word:warka)**, and the water gums **[dakumbar](word:dakumbar)** and **[jinajina](word:jinajina)**, the latter 'good timber for woomeras' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Cooktown name for the bloodwood whose bark made troughs was *jin-jil* (Guugu Yimithirr); on the Palmer the Koko-minni called the inland bloodwood *ga-ja*, and at Princess Charlotte Bay it was *richindi* [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1903]. Palmer's Cloncurry name for the inland bloodwood was *Narm-boon-bong* and on the Gilbert *Kulcha*; the gall was *Kurcha* 'on the Mitchell and Cloncurry Rivers', in languages he does not name [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: The bloodwoods of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
Bloodwoods are the genus *Corymbia*, split from *Eucalyptus* in 1995, and the rough-barked ones share a look: bark 'tessellated', cracked into small plates, on the trunk and branches; leaves paler underneath; flowers in branched bunches of seven at the ends of the twigs; and big thick-walled fruit shaped like an urn or a barrel, with a winged seed [ref:euclid-clarksoniana] [ref:wiki-erythrophloia]. Cut one and it bleeds red kino, the 'blood' [ref:wiki-terminalis].

**Clarkson's bloodwood** (*C. clarksoniana*) is the woodland's: a tree to 15 m with a lignotuber, bark 'rough throughout, tessellated, grey, grey-brown and red to orange', glossy green lance-shaped leaves 6–18 cm long, cream flowers, and fruit 'urceolate varying to barrel-shaped', 1.2–2.5 cm long. It grows 'as a component of often grassy woodlands and forests on sand and sandy loam, but also may be on rising ground in skeletal soil', from northern New South Wales to about 13° on the Peninsula; flowering is recorded in January and from March to August [ref:euclid-clarksoniana]. The Queensland Herbarium's description of the hill woodland at Karma Waters names it with Molloy red box and Cullen's ironbark as the three trees of the slopes [ref:re-woodland].

**Red bloodwood** (*C. erythrophloia*), 'variable-barked' or 'gum-topped bloodwood': to 15 m, with 'tessellated, red-brown, dull, grey or pink bark that is persistent on the trunk and lower branches' and sheds 'in small polygonal flakes giving the tree a mottled appearance'; it runs from Cooktown west to the Gulf and south to Hervey Bay, often with narrow-leaved ironbark [ref:wiki-erythrophloia].

**Hyland's bloodwood** (*C. hylandii*) on the sandstone and granite ridges and **blotchy bloodwood** (*C. stockeri*) on the river levees are the other two common ones here; the [woodland](entry:woodland) page sets them side by side [ref:wiki-hylandii] [ref:wiki-stockeri].

**Inland bloodwood** (*C. terminalis*), tjuta, the bloodwood of the dry country, reaches the upper Mitchell: a tree to 18 m 'on river flats, scree slopes and dune swales', with light brown to light grey tessellated bark and scurfy cream buds. Its flowers 'produce drops of nectar which provide a high energy food source for many desert animals including honeyeaters, insects and possums', and it carries the bush coconut, a gall made by a coccid insect that 'burrows into the bark', which 'must be broken open; the insect on the inside can be eaten, and contains a lot of moisture' [ref:wiki-terminalis].

**The smooth ones.** The same genus holds the smooth-barked gums of the flats: Dallachy's ghost gum (*C. dallachiana*), the commonest tree in the Karma Waters records, with 'smooth white to cream-coloured and pinkish bark that is shed in thin patches' on the grassy plains and creek levees, and the carbeens *C. confertiflora* and *C. tessellaris* with a rough grey stocking at the base and smooth limbs above [ref:wiki-dallachiana] [ref:wiki-confertiflora] [ref:wiki-tessellaris] [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: Bloodwood, ironbark, box
sections.body:
- **Bloodwood**: bark in small squares, flaking, grey to red; urn-shaped fruit as big as a thumb-joint; red kino [ref:euclid-clarksoniana] [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- **[Ironbark](entry:woodland)** (Cullen's): bark hard, black, deeply furrowed, never flaking; small fruit [ref:re-woodland].
- **Box** (Molloy red box, green-leaf box): bark fibrous and flaky in short strips, grey-brown; small cup fruit [ref:re-woodland].
- **Ghost gum and carbeen**: bark smooth and white or with a rough grey stocking only at the base; these are bloodwoods too, by the fruit and the flower bunches, but no one calls them that [ref:wiki-dallachiana] [ref:wiki-tessellaris].
- **[Ironwood](entry:ironwood)**: not a gum at all; dark, hard, rough bark, pinnate leaves and a flat pod [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Among the bloodwoods**, the fruit shape is the best guide: Clarkson's urn-shaped and less than twice as long as wide; Hyland's smaller; the inland bloodwood scurfy-budded [ref:euclid-clarksoniana] [ref:wiki-terminalis].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Red stains** down the trunk where a limb has broken: kino [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- **Chewed fruit** split open under a tree is cockatoo work; eucalypt seed, 'especially the big-fruited gums and bloodwoods', is the mainstay of the red-tailed black cockatoo [ref:wiki-rtbc].
- **Galls** as big as a hen's egg on the young trees, Palmer's *Kurcha*, with a grub or a bag of jelly inside [ref:palmer1883].
- **A white crust on the leaves and twigs** after the rains is manna, which Palmer saw gathered on the Mitchell [ref:palmer1883].
- **Bee dung at the base and a hollow note when tapped** mark a [sugarbag](entry:native-bees) tree; big old bloodwoods with hollows are the hives [ref:anderson1996].
- **Bark scars**, long and rectangular, on old trees by a camp are trough scars [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Where they grow
sections.body: Clarkson's bloodwood on the sandy and stony slopes with the ironbark and the red box; Hyland's on the sandstone and granite ridges; the blotchy bloodwood on the river levees; the inland bloodwood on the flats toward the dry country; the ghost gum on the grassy plains and creek levees [ref:re-woodland] [ref:wiki-hylandii] [ref:wiki-stockeri] [ref:wiki-terminalis] [ref:wiki-dallachiana]. All of them are trees of grassy woodland on sand and sandy loam, which is the country of the upper Mitchell at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) [ref:euclid-clarksoniana] [ref:re-woodland]. The dictionary's bloodwood words come from the open country behind the Bloomfield, the eastern edge of the same woodland [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: What the bloodwood feeds
sections.body: The bloodwood is a nectar tree and a hollow tree. Its flowers feed the honeyeaters, the [flying foxes](entry:woodland) and the [native bees](entry:native-bees), whose sugarbag fills its hollows; its seed feeds the red-tailed black cockatoo, which can be heard cracking the fruit from a long way off; its galls feed the grub and the people who found them; and its manna, the sugary exudate that follows the rains, was food on the Mitchell [ref:wiki-terminalis] [ref:wiki-rtbc] [ref:palmer1883]. The hollows that the kino and the termites make in an old bloodwood are the nest sites of the [woodland](entry:woodland): parrots, kookaburras, possums, bats, goannas [ref:re-woodland]. Fire runs under it every few years in this country, and the tessellated bark and the lignotuber are what let it stand through the burns [ref:pbg-cape-york] [ref:euclid-clarksoniana].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Clarkson's bloodwood flowers from March to August and in January, so its blossom and its sugarbag run through the dry [ref:euclid-clarksoniana]. Palmer: 'After the rainy season this food is said to be abundant', of the manna [ref:palmer1883]. Bark comes off 'at the end of the wet season when the sap is up and the bark slips' [ref:roth1904]. Seed falls to the cockatoos in the late dry. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Bark troughs.** At Cooktown the spiked pleat-type trough was made from the bark of the bloodwood (*jin-jil*), among other trees; see [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) [ref:roth1904].
- **Windbreak.** Leafy bloodwood boughs thrown down in a half circle round the sleeping place; see [huts and shelters](entry:huts-and-shelters) [ref:roth1910-huts].
- **Hair.** At Bloomfield, 'small clay balls mixed with bloodwood seed pods' were put into the hair with beeswax [ref:anderson1996].
- **Charcoal.** Bloodwood charcoal was a body paint on the Tully and a wound dressing at Brisbane, where a washed and scraped wound 'would then just be covered up with wood-ashes or blood-wood charcoal' [ref:roth1903].
- **Kino as medicine, elsewhere.** On the Palmer the Koko-minni took the inland bloodwood's gum 'mixed with water ... for constipation'; in the Boulia, Cloncurry and Georgina districts the bloodwood gum was dusted on sores or boiled and drunk; in the desert the kino is drunk in water for diarrhoea, indigestion and chest pain. No Kuku Yalanji medicinal use of kino is on record [ref:roth1903] [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- **Cement.** At Brisbane 'this "bloodwood" gum was warmed for use, and mixed with spittle to make it set' [ref:roth1904].
- **Manna.** On the Mitchell the sugary particles were gathered from the leaves and small branches laid on bark, 'or are scraped off with mussel-shells into a kooliman', or the crusted leaves were 'pounded together with a stone and roasted in the ashes' [ref:palmer1883].
- **Galls.** The *Kurcha* galls on young bloodwood and messmate, 'two inches or more in diameter', with a grub or 'a small transparent bag of jelly-like substance' inside, were eaten on the Mitchell; the inland bloodwood's bush coconut is the same thing [ref:palmer1883] [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- **Timber.** The inland bloodwood's wood 'was used by indigenous peoples to make spear-throwers, digging bowls and carrying vessels' [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- **Sugarbag** from the hollows; see [native bees](entry:native-bees) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Working the bloodwood
sections.body:
**Manna** (Palmer's Mitchell River method) [ref:palmer1883]: after the rains, when the leaves and twigs carry a white crust, lay sheets of bark under the tree and strip the leaves onto them so the particles fall; or scrape the crust off with a mussel shell into a trough; or pound the crusted leaves with a stone and roast the mass in the ashes.

**Galls**: break the big gall open; eat the grub or the jelly inside [ref:palmer1883] [ref:wiki-terminalis].

**A bark trough**: the Cooktown method is on the [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) page; take the sheet when the sap is up after the storms [ref:roth1904].

**Charcoal**: bloodwood charcoal, cold and crushed, for paint or a dressing [ref:roth1903].

**Finding sugarbag**: in the late dry, check the bases of the old bloodwoods for bee dung and tap the trunks for hollowness; see [native bees](entry:native-bees) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Old bloodwoods drop limbs; never camp under a dead one [ref:kw-camping].
- The kino medicines on record are from other districts and other languages; the Kuku Yalanji record is silent, and this page does not recommend them [ref:roth1903] [ref:wiki-terminalis].
- Cutting bark or felling on the station is a matter for the lessee's permission; scarred trees are protected heritage [ref:kw-about] [ref:acha2003].
- Fire: this is a 2–5 year burn woodland, and a bloodwood crown fire in the late dry is not a cultural burn [ref:pbg-cape-york] [ref:qfd].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The bloodwoods are the most ordinary trees on Karma Waters and the ones with the most in them: the cockatoos, the bees, the hollows, the kino and the galls. Which of the three dictionary words belongs to which tree is a question for Kuku Yalanji speakers; the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982]. Gathering on native title country is protected by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* and recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].
